segs.text: Module three, objective six. Choosing the infusion rate that gives a desired steady state concentration. The infusion rate, R, is the amount of drug put in per hour; C s s is the plateau concentration, where the rate in equals the rate out; and the clearance is the volume of plasma emptied of drug per hour. The question is which R puts the plateau at a target level.

At the plateau, the amount eliminated each hour is the clearance times the level, and it equals the amount going in. So the rate needed is the amount the patient eliminates each hour at the target level: R equals C s s times clearance. A higher target needs a proportionally higher rate, because at a higher level more drug leaves each hour. A patient with a lower clearance, as in renal failure, needs a proportionally lower rate for the same target, because less drug leaves each hour at that level. Once the clearance is known, V D, the apparent volume of distribution, adds nothing to this choice: the volume on its own decides the loading dose, not the rate.

card.m: Cl falls → R falls in proportion
her Practice 4: Cl 11.55 → 8.55 L/hr, R 115.5 → 85.5 mg/hr
V<sub>D</sub>: sets the loading dose, not R

segs.text: Changing R moves the plateau and nothing else. Raising R raises C s s in proportion, but the plateau still arrives at the same time, because that time depends only on the half-life. She said, All we're doing is shifting that curve upward. She also said, changing the rate changes our steady state concentration, and said she repeated it five times on purpose. In her review, fifty milligrams per hour gave about twelve milligrams per liter and one hundred gave twenty four, each reached in three to five half-lives.

card.m: R raised → C<sub>ss</sub> raised, same time to the plateau
her review: 50 → 100 mg/hr, C<sub>ss</sub> 12 → 24 mg/L, both in 3 to 5 half-lives

segs.text: The equation sheet gives C s s equals R over clearance; rearranged, R equals C s s times clearance. C s s is on the top, so the rate rises with the target, and the clearance is on the top, so the rate rises with the clearance. When the stem gives a half-life and a volume, the clearance is k, the fraction eliminated per hour, times V D, so R equals C s s times k times V D; V D appears only as part of the clearance. Milligrams per liter times liters per hour leaves milligrams per hour, an amount per time. If the stem gives a solution concentration, R is converted to milliliters per hour or per minute for the pump.

card.m: R = C<sub>ss</sub> × k × V<sub>D</sub>, with k × V<sub>D</sub> = Cl

segs.text: Her slide Example two asks the rate that gives a C s s of twenty milligrams per liter for the Example one drug: half-life six hours, V D thirty liters. R equals C s s times clearance, and the stem gives no clearance, so it is built as k times thirty liters. Twenty milligrams per liter times that clearance, three point four six five liters per hour, is sixty nine point three milligrams per hour. As a check, sixty nine point three over the clearance gives back twenty milligrams per liter. In Example one, fifty milligrams per hour gave fourteen point four three milligrams per liter; rate and level are in proportion, so between the two examples both rose by the same factor, one point three eight six.

card.m: t<sub>½</sub> = 6 hr, V<sub>D</sub> = 30 L; target C<sub>ss</sub> = 20 mg/L: R = ?

segs.text: In her review the target is twenty four milligrams per liter, the half-life five hours and V D about twenty two liters. k is zero point one three eight six per hour, so R is twenty four times k times twenty two, seventy three point one eight milligrams per hour, which she gives as about seventy three. Her graded quiz asked for a rate to reach twenty three micrograms per milliliter with a V D of fifteen liters and a four hour half-life; micrograms per milliliter equal milligrams per liter, and the key is sixty milligrams per hour. The word recommend means round to a number a pump could take. The loading dose that goes with this rate, C s s times V D, is objective four.

card.m: C<sub>ss</sub> = 24 mg/L, t<sub>½</sub> = 5 hr, V<sub>D</sub> ≈ 22 L
recommend → a number a pump could take

segs.text: How she tests it: a target C s s and two of the parameters, the half-life or k, and V D or the clearance. With a solution concentration in the stem, a parallel part asks the rate in volume: zero point three five milliliters per minute in her Practice one, and one point three two milliliters per hour from one hundred twenty five milligram per milliliter vials in Practice two. The distractor she flags is that a different rate reaches steady state sooner. It does not, because the time depends only on the half-life, and the half-life depends on the clearance and V D, not on the rate. While working Example two aloud she called the thirty liters the clearance; thirty liters is V D.
